strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: benchmarks for LLM code security suffer from contamination and require substantial manual effort to extend. An automated pipeline for bootstrapping scenario/test/exploit triplets in the BaxBench format is a useful contribution to the community.

Validation is unusually thorough for a benchmark-generation paper: (i) pipeline outputs are compared against human-expert artifacts on the same BaxBench scenarios, with confusion matrices on both pass@1 (83.5% agreement, precision 81.6%, recall 81.1%) and sec_pass@1; (ii) a structured expert study with 4 security experts on 12 scenarios reports average scores and inter-rater agreement (Table 4); (iii) an ablation replaces the orchestration/solution LLMs and checks for generation bias; (iv) a CWE-400 ablation quantifies the effect of including the weakest exploit class.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations: it reports that the generating model (Claude-4.5 Sonnet) scores substantially higher on self-generated scenarios (95.2% vs 80.8% pass@1), that CWE-400 exploits are unreliable (and excludes them with an ablation), that only 81% of CWE classifications are judged correct, and that exploit coverage is rated only 71%. It even documents pipeline failure modes (B.2) and reports two incorrect tests found in BaxBench itself.

Reproducibility support is strong: algorithms, per-step prompts (App. C), token/cost breakdowns, per-scenario statistics, and a released benchmark of 40 novel scenarios across three difficulty tiers, at a very low per-scenario cost (~USD 4).

The demonstration that the method finds exploits missed by human experts (e.g., OS Injection in FileSearch) with concrete evidence in App. A.4 is a convincing qualitative illustration that the approach can exceed expert-written tests, not merely match them.
weaknesses: Several central claims rest on partially single-annotator evidence. The '71 security exploits, only one unsound' finding and the 'same quality, if not more comprehensive' claim lean on manual annotation by one author, with the follow-up expert study limited to a sample of 6 scenarios (later 12 in App. A.5). Independent multi-annotator verification of all generated tasks would be needed to fully support the claim of matching expert-written tests.

The demonstrated generation bias is material: Claude-4.5 Sonnet performs 14+ points better on its self-generated benchmark than on the GPT-5-generated one, for both pass@1 and sec_pass@1. The ablation is small (3-4 scenarios), so the magnitude and generality of this bias for future users of the pipeline (who will likely use whatever frontier model is available) is under-characterized. This weakens the claim that automatically generated benchmarks are neutral evaluation instruments.

The validation against BaxBench treats BaxBench as ground truth while simultaneously finding two of its functional tests wrong and one specification ambiguous; the 16.5% disagreement on pass@1 is explained, but the correction of BaxBench tests by the authors of this paper introduces a circularity risk in the comparative evaluation. No third-party adjudication is reported.

The security-side soundness story ('no false positives, sound upper bound') is complicated by the paper's own findings: experts raised false-positive concerns for some non-CWE-400 exploits, CWE classification is only 81% correct, and coverage is rated low with very poor inter-rater agreement (22.58%). sec_pass@1 numbers should therefore be interpreted cautiously, which the paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve.

The novel benchmark is modest in scale (40 scenarios; the HARD split is only 10) and generated with a single orchestration model, so conclusions about difficulty scaling and subset construction from such a small sample have limited statistical support.

Originality is moderate: the technical core is a careful agentic refinement pipeline (execution-feedback iteration, hardened/weakened solution regularization, judge-based verdicts) built from known techniques (self-debugging, self-criticism, LLM-as-judge). The novelty lies in the application domain and validation rather than in a new method.

Presentation has notable blemishes that reduce polish: typos ('security tets', 'sustained security evaluation of evaluation of LLM-based code generation'), duplicated SWT-bench references (2024a/2024b), a release URL left blank ('release the scenarios at .'), and Figure 2/25/24 captions that appear copy-pasted or mismatched (Figures 24 and 25 captions are identical despite showing different content).
